Physics, objects & tools across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Object modeling

From ages 12 to 25, object understanding undergoes a fundamental transformation: it shifts from being primarily about recognition to being about system identification-inferring the latent parameters of objects that matter for prediction and control. By early adulthood, perceiving an object increasingly means building an implicit model of its behavior under manipulation.

Adolescents develop increasingly precise prediction of material properties (stiffness, brittleness, friction, viscosity, density) from sparse visual and tactile cues. Where a child might need to handle an object to know how it behaves, adults achieve seamless cross-modal prediction: visual inspection alone yields accurate expectations about how an object will feel, sound when struck, deform under load, or slide across a surface. Alongside this, viewpoint-invariant recognition becomes faster and more robust. Adults maintain stable object identity across dramatic changes in viewing angle, lighting, and partial occlusion, reflecting increasingly abstract, geometry-based representations rather than view-dependent templates.

From 12-25, "material understanding" also expands beyond mostly rigid-body expectations into increasingly accurate intuitions for deformable and flowing matter. Adolescents-to-adults get better at predicting the behavior of cloth, rope, rubber, dough, and other soft bodies whose shape changes continuously under contact, and of fluids and granular materials whose dynamics depend sensitively on containment geometry and motion history. Mature perception increasingly infers not just a single "hard/soft" label, but latent parameters that matter for control (compliance, internal damping, yield thresholds, stickiness, viscosity, surface tension, and packing density) so a quick visual/tactile sample can support actionable forecasts (how fabric will drape or snag, how batter will pour or "glug," how sand will slump or avalanche). These domains recruit different computational primitives than rigid scenes (continuous deformation fields, boundary conditions, and state that is history-dependent) so their refinement represents a real broadening of the world model’s representational basis, and it matters for adult-relevant skills like cooking, cleanup, cable/rope handling, material transport, and packaging.

Another key object-centric developmental achievement is hidden structure inference; adolescents become increasingly capable of inferring whether an object is hollow versus solid, whether it contains moving parts, and what internal mechanisms might explain its behavior. More broadly, object representations become compositional. Rather than encoding objects as holistic gestalts, the mature system represents them as assemblies of parts with distinct functional subsystems. These factorized representations decompose objects into parts, joints, materials, and contact surfaces, enabling understanding of the causal role each component plays in overall function. This supports intervention prediction (e.g anticipating what happens when you remove a screw, block a vent, or swap a gear ratio) and counterfactual rollouts that mentally simulate alternative configurations. This is where intuitive physics begins to look more like intuitive engineering, with reasoning organized around constraints, forces, failure modes, and parameter sensitivities rather than surface-level behavior descriptions.

A closely related refinement is the maturation of containment and support intuitions: reasoning about what can fit inside what, what can stably rest on what, and how objects nest, stack, and constrain each other. By early adulthood, agents become better at inferring clearance, orientation-dependence, and tolerance margins from sparse views (will this box fit in that drawer if rotated; does the opening taper; is there an internal obstruction), and at predicting stability from geometry + mass distribution + contact mechanics (where the center of mass projects, how friction limits sliding, whether a load path concentrates stress, whether a shelf will sag or a stack will topple). Importantly, these judgments become uncertainty-aware and probe-driven: adults increasingly represent margins ("it fits, but barely") and deploy low-cost test actions (test-fit, gentle preload, wiggle, partial stack) before committing to irreversible placements. This constraint-focused containment/support modeling is heavily recruited in packing, organizing, construction, moving furniture through doorways, and any task where spatial reasoning must be coupled to mechanical feasibility.

Category knowledge becomes more functional and relational, which is why adults can transfer skills across unfamiliar objects. Instead of "this thing looks like X," you lean on "this is clamp-like," "this is lever-like," "this fastener behaves like M3 threads," or "it’s a pump because it moves fluid via this mechanism." Hierarchies become easier to traverse (basic <-> subordinate <-> superordinate) because categories carry deeper explanatory structure: materials, manufacturing processes, typical internal components, and causal histories. A key amplifier here is learning from symbolic artifacts (manuals, schematics, exploded diagrams, CAD-like views) and grounding them into action; the model becomes easier to update from language and diagrams, not just trial-and-error interaction.

On the "object physics" side, adolescents-to-adults improve both fidelity and compression. Predictions for collisions, projectiles, balance points, and multi-body interactions become more reliable, but the more important shift is representational: moving from local, ad hoc explanations ("it fell because it’s heavy") toward latent-variable models ("net torque about the pivot is clockwise; mass distribution increased moment of inertia; friction coefficient bounds the tangential impulse") that generalize across objects and contexts. You get better at coordinating multiple constraints at once (force + leverage + friction + timing), using explicit stabilizers when needed (diagrams, coordinate frames, equations), and tracking second-order effects that bite in real mechanisms (backlash, compliance, thermal expansion, resonance, stick-slip). Energy becomes a unifying abstraction rather than a classroom fact: you more automatically reason about energy storage and transfer across domains (elastic <-> kinetic <-> thermal), which supports better "debugging" of physical systems via "what if I changed X?" counterfactuals and clearer separation of correlation from mechanism.

A crucial late refinement is that intuitive physics becomes explicitly uncertainty-aware and robustness-seeking. Adults increasingly represent not just point predictions ("it will hold") but confidence, bounds, and tail risks ("it will probably hold, but the failure mode is catastrophic"). This shifts action selection toward conservative, risk-sensitive control policies: using safety margins, choosing redundant supports, preferring stable grasps and wide base-of-support postures, and running low-cost "probe" actions (tap, wiggle, partial load, small test cut) before committing to irreversible or dangerous moves. In effect, the world model starts carrying distributional predictions over outcomes and failure modes, so planning optimizes expected utility under uncertainty rather than raw accuracy.

Relatedly, objects become modeled as time-evolving systems with tolerances, wear, and maintenance states rather than static ideal mechanisms. Adolescents learn that a screw either tightens or doesn’t; adults learn to expect drift: threads strip, blades dull, bearings develop play, batteries sag, adhesives creep, materials fatigue, and friction changes with dust, oil, water, and temperature. Mature object models therefore include latent "health" variables (clearance, sharpness, compliance, lubrication, remaining safety factor) and reason in terms of tolerance stacks and failure envelopes, not just nominal geometry. This is a key reason adult intuitive physics looks less like textbook Newtonian scenes and more like operating on degraded, imperfect artifacts in the wild.

Finally, from 12-25, objects become increasingly modeled as socially-embedded entities, not just physical ones. Ownership, norms, value, provenance, coordination rules, taboos, and replacement cost get fused into the representation because they change action selection: who can use it, what counts as damage, what’s fair, what’s risky, what signals status, what’s expensive or hard to repair. Overall, mature object understanding is less about naming things and more about inferring the latent structure that governs how they behave (physically and socially) so you can predict, intervene, and coordinate with minimal friction.

Tool use

The refinements in object modeling described above directly enable a qualitative shift in tool use. By early adulthood, affordance perception becomes richly conditional: rather than treating an object’s action possibilities as fixed properties, the mature system computes affordances as functions of context, goal, and body state. A chair is not simply "sittable" but "can be stood on if the surface is dry, if my shoes grip, if the load is under X kg, if I place my feet near the base." This conditionalization extends to hierarchical affordances, where objects are understood almost like APIs, with preconditions, parameters, and action sequences (open -> orient -> insert -> twist) that must be executed in the correct order to achieve the desired effect. A developmental experiment examines body representation after tool use (Figure) 2. The study compares movement kinematics across puberty (Figure). The researchers measure reach kinematics before and after tool use (Figure). The same study analyzes grasping movements (Figure). The study measures perceived arm length (Figure).

Underlying this is a strengthening of causal models for tool-object-environment interactions. Adolescents develop increasingly sophisticated failure diagnosis: "it’s binding because alignment is off," "the bit is slipping because torque exceeds friction," "the adhesive failed because of surface contamination." This causal depth supports planning of multi-step transformations ( e.g measure -> mark -> cut -> sand -> fit) where each operation changes the state space for subsequent ones. Motor preparation itself becomes more anticipatory: pre-shaping of grip and posture increasingly reflects not just current object state but the future states that will result from planned actions. This diagnosis also becomes uncertainty- and wear-aware: you consider whether the tool is dull, out of spec, miscalibrated, or heat-soaked, and you choose interventions that are robust to parameter drift (slower feed rate, more lubrication, different bit geometry, a jig to reduce variance); mature tool use explicitly manages failure probability, trading speed for safety margin when the cost of error is high, and using small "test" actions to collapse uncertainty before full commitment.

More broadly, tool use becomes deeply hierarchical in its temporal organization. Planning extends across minutes to hours, safety constraints are managed proactively rather than reactively, measuring instruments are deployed to close feedback loops, and external scaffolds (i.e checklists, jigs, fixtures, software macros) are constructed to offload cognitive load and reduce error. Tool selection also becomes more optimal, with choices reflecting nuanced task demands (material hardness, required precision, access constraints) rather than habit or mere availability.

A related development is improved ability to overcome functional fixedness, seeing familiar objects as candidates for novel uses. More impressively, tool chains emerge: using tools to create or modify other tools (second-order tool use), adjusting and improvising tools for better task fit, and occasionally inventing novel tools or novel applications entirely; while true tool innovation remains rare, the underlying cognitive capacity is present by early adulthood.

With extended practice, frequently used tools undergo phenomenological integration: they become "transparent" extensions of the body schema rather than external objects requiring explicit attention. This tool-body integration enables the fluid, automatic manipulation characteristic of expertise. Expertise also drives the development of domain-specific object ontologies: the carpenter, mechanic, surgeon, and programmer each acquire rich categorical structures for the tools of their trade, organized around function, failure modes, and interoperability rather than surface appearance. Overall, mature tool use reflects not just improved dexterity but a deeper representational infrastructure, one that models tools as mediators between intention and world state, embedded in causal webs that extend across time, objects, and social context. A 2026 experiment tests tactile localization through a tool (Figure) 1. The study varies arm posture (Figure).

Gross motor

From 12 to 25, gross motor skill shifts from "execute a learned movement" toward robust, model-based control of the whole body in dynamic, uncertain environments. A central gain is predictive control: adolescents increasingly learn to anticipate where their body will be in the near future (tens to hundreds of milliseconds ahead) and to plan actions that keep the system stable under expected forces and delays. This shows up as tighter timing and rhythmic coordination, better exploitation of momentum, and more reliable coupling between perception and action in high-speed tasks where late corrections are too costly (sports, driving, fast navigation through crowds). In parallel, balance becomes less fragile: postural control improves not just for quiet standing, but for perturbations-slips, trips, bumps, sudden load shifts-where the mature system can rapidly infer the disturbance, select an appropriate recovery strategy, and re-stabilize with minimal conscious intervention. Arm anatomy provides a structural frame for understanding body-centered action maps (Figure).

Another qualitative change is that gross motor increasingly becomes multi-agent and spatially strategic. Many adult-relevant movements are not solo "skills" but coordinated control in shared space: reading others’ trajectories, predicting collision risks, and shaping your own motion to manage spacing, feints, handoffs, and mutual constraints (whether in sports or mundane tasks like carrying a couch through a doorway). Here, the motor system is not only controlling limbs; it is running a local planner over a moving obstacle field composed of other people, with social priors about how they will yield, accelerate, or commit. Relatedly, the ability to predict terrain and support surfaces improves: with sparse visual cues (lighting, texture, slope, wetness) and brief tactile samples (foot contact, vibration), adults become better at inferring stability and friction and adjusting gait, foot placement, and posture proactively rather than learning by near-falls. Finally, adult gross motor integrates biomechanics with higher-level goals: posture and lifting become optimized around constraints like leverage, spinal loading, fatigue management, and injury risk, and "what to do" (strategy) blends more seamlessly with "how to do it" (execution). In mature performance, planning, perception, and motor control stop feeling like separate stages and instead act like one integrated controller that continuously trades off speed, safety, precision, and effort in real time. A youth soccer study tests augmented feedback (Figure) 3. The study compares motor performance across training groups (Figure). The researchers assess skill retention (Figure). The study breaks performance down by drill (Figure).

Fine motor

From 12 to 25, fine motor control shifts from basic competence to optimized, context-sensitive precision. A central development is improved calibration of the speed-accuracy tradeoff. Adolescents and young adults learn when to slow down for precision versus when speed is acceptable, and this calibration becomes increasingly personal and task-aware. A child might approach all writing tasks at roughly the same pace; an adult automatically shifts between rapid note-scribbling, careful form-filling, and painstaking signature on a legal document-each reflecting an implicit cost-benefit analysis of error consequences. This shows up across domains: knowing when a soldering joint demands extra steadiness, when a brushstroke can be fast and loose versus deliberate, or when typing speed matters more than typo rate.

Alongside this, haptic-motor integration becomes more sophisticated. Fine motor actions increasingly exploit rich tactile feedback to guide real-time microadjustments: feeling the "give" of a screw approaching its seat (and backing off before stripping), sensing when a pencil needs more or less pressure as paper texture changes, detecting the moment a needle pierces fabric, or adjusting grip force as a wet glass begins to slip. These feedback loops tighten with development, enabling smoother, more reliable control without visual monitoring: threading a needle while watching the fabric, touch-typing without looking at keys, or adjusting a pipette by feel alone.

Another noteworthy feature of this period is that fine motor gains become increasingly domain-specific. The musician develops finger independence and microsecond timing precision; the surgeon acquires tremor suppression and steady control under magnification; the artist refines pressure modulation and stroke dynamics; the competitive gamer hones rapid, precise thumb movements. The same individual may possess expert-level fine motor skill in one domain while remaining unremarkable in another, reflecting how practice sculpts highly specialized sensorimotor circuits rather than a single "general dexterity" factor.

Finally, a key late development is the capacity to rapidly acquire novel sensorimotor mappings. Adults can adapt to a new keyboard layout, adjust to different mouse sensitivity settings, learn to control an unfamiliar video game controller, or master a novel surgical instrument far more efficiently than children. This reflects a more flexible motor learning system, one that can quickly build internal models of new tool dynamics and remap intentions onto unfamiliar output channels. Where a child might need extensive repetition, the adult motor system leverages abstract structure (this tool is "joystick-like," this interface is "trackpad-like") to bootstrap learning, achieving functional competence in hours rather than weeks.

Knowledge compilation and compounding

From 12 to 25, a major change is that physical competence becomes increasingly compiled: consciously/explicitly initiated and monitored control ("keep your wrist straight," "apply torque gradually," "listen for the pitch change") is progressively transformed into procedural control policies that run as fast, low-attention "macros." Through automatization and hierarchical chunking, component actions that were once consciously monitored get bundled into reliable subroutines (grasp →\rightarrow align →\rightarrow load →\rightarrow release; measure →\rightarrow mark →\rightarrow cut →\rightarrow fit), so working memory is freed to track higher-level goals, constraints, and outcomes. This compilation is not just about speed; it increases robustness by stabilizing the invariants that matter (timing relations, contact transitions, force ramps), allowing attention to shift from how to move toward whether the world is behaving as expected-exactly the division of labor that makes expert tool use feel "transparent" rather than effortful.

The deeper developmental jump is that skill acquisition itself becomes more self-engineered and therefore compounding. Adolescents-to-adults increasingly learn how to learn sensorimotor skills: they decompose tasks into subskills, invent drills that isolate failure modes, and use deliberate feedback channels (slow-motion video, metronomes, measurements, checklists, jigs/fixtures) to close loops and reduce variance. Concurrently, the system builds "structural learning" priors (abstract knowledge about classes of dynamics) so mastery transfers: learning one compliant, underdamped interaction (a springy tool, a flexible material) makes the next one cheaper because you’re reusing a latent model family rather than starting from scratch.

A final refinement concerns the precision of forward models and the resulting sense of agency; efference-copy predictions cancel expected self-generated sensations with tighter error bars, so small deviations pop out as anomalies ("the bit is slipping," "alignment is off," "the joint is binding," "this vibration isn’t mine") and can be more accurately tagged as self-generated error or external perturbations. This precision has direct functional consequences: it enables reliable anomaly detection during tool use, supports the phenomenological "transparency" of well-practiced implements, and underlies the robust sense of authorship over one’s own actions that grounds both adaptive motor control and coordination with others. Essentially, mature motor learning increasingly looks like self-supervised prediction + anomaly detection layered on hierarchical control-supporting both faster transfer and better fault diagnosis when tools, materials, or your own body drift out of spec.
